## Conflicts carried by the reports themselves (16)

Each is a passage in which the report states two readings or contradicts another passage; carry every reading as a selectable scenario.

- `NPSX-CLI-PCB-p082-03` Shefferer farm field (Warfield Ridge) (NPS-CLI-PCB p. Page 77 of 131): The use of the Shefferer field in 1863 is uncertain: young orchard, or crops or meadow; open in either case
- `NPSX-CLI-PCB-p117-01` Sherfy Fields 1, 2 and 5 fence type (NPS-CLI-PCB p. PDF 117): The narrative from Barksdale's Brigade, published 51 years after the battle, supports a post and rail fence type and the circa 1890 Tipton photograph a post and slab fence type for the Sherfy field fences; the report says the differences may reflect variations in terminology, challenges with memory, or different iterations of fence construction over time
- `NPSX-CLI-1STDAY-p060-10` Forney Field 5, eastern fence line (NPS-CLI-1STDAY p. Page 58 of 105): The documentation of the 1863 eastern fence line of Forney Field 5 is not conclusive
- `NPSX-CLI-1STDAY-p060-12` Forney Field 6, eastern fence line (NPS-CLI-1STDAY p. Page 58 of 105): The documentation of the 1863 eastern fence line of Forney Field 6 is not conclusive
- `NPSX-CLR-1STDAY-p072-01` Harman farm orchard: possibly post-battle (NPS-CLR-1STDAY p. 50): The report notes that the orchard shown surrounding the side of the Harman brick house could be a post-battle addition, since no claims for damage to it were filed
- `NPSX-CLR-1STDAY-p424-03` Gilbert orchard (species not known) (NPS-CLR-1STDAY p. 396): An orchard of unknown species occupied the field south of McClean Grove on the Gilbert outlot (Gilbert Field #1), while the report elsewhere places the apple orchard in the northern outlot next to the McClean farm
- `NPSX-CLR-1STDAY-p369-01` Dustman (Lee's headquarters) orchard: five acres (NPS-CLR-1STDAY p. 341): Casper Dustman leased or owned a five-acre orchard west of the seminary, where Lee's headquarters operations were housed in tents after July 1 (the report elsewhere calls the orchard lot four acres)
- `NPSX-ADHI-p037-01` First Minnesota Memorial of 1867 (NPS-ADHI p. PDF 37): In 1867 the first monument/memorial in both the national cemetery and the battlefield was the 1st Minnesota Memorial, which antedated the Soldiers' National Monument by two years (the executive summary of the same report dates the first monuments on the battlefield later: see the entry on the first monuments)
- `NPSX-CLR-LRT-p021-01` When the west slope was cleared is not confirmed (NPS-CLR-LRT p. PDF 21): Many later secondary sources say the timber was cleared the year before the battle, but this is not confirmed by any known primary source; photographs taken after the battle show considerable secondary growth (various shrubs) and some scattered medium-size oaks and pines, and it seems likely that substantial portions of the hill had been cleared some years before the battle, perhaps as early as 1858 when Hanaway acquired the land
- `NPSX-CLR-LRT-p125-03` Breastworks in front of the 16th Michigan said to have been built on the night of July 3 by Crawford's division, not there at the time of the battle (NPS-CLR-LRT p. PDF 125): Calvin Hamilton wrote on 10 October 1892, in a letter quoted by the report, that the stone breastworks in front of the 16th Michigan line were thrown up on the night of 3 July 1863 principally by Crawford's Division, that they were not there at the time of the battle on July 2 at that point, and that survivors of Crawford's division living at Gettysburg helped to throw them up; this differs from the accounts that put the building of stone works on the night of July 2 or the afternoon of July 2
- `NPSX-CLR-LRT-p061-01` Tablet beside the breastworks east of Sykes Avenue: wall built for defense July 3 P.M. 1863 (NPS-CLR-LRT p. PDF 61): The report quotes a smaller tablet standing at the edge of a breastworks just east of Sykes Avenue which reads that the wall was built for defense on July 3 P.M. 1863; the report elsewhere says the breastworks were hastily constructed on the night of July 2
- `NPSX-CLR-LRT-p073-01` 146th New York erected stone wall breastworks on the afternoon of July 2 (monument entry) (NPS-CLR-LRT p. PDF 73): The report's entry for the 146th New York monument says the regiment deployed there and erected stone wall breastworks on the afternoon of July 2, 1863 and remained until the end of the battle; a regimental commander's report quoted elsewhere in the same report says the stone wall was built at night
- `NPSX-HARMON-FARM-p035-01` Harman brick house said to have survived the fire; Elliott map shows barn and outbuildings burned (NPS-HARMON-FARM p. PDF 35): The study says the Elliott map (surveyed August-November 1863) shows the barn and outbuildings burned but not the house, so the brick house seems to have survived, a 1870s photograph showing a brick house with an orchard but no outbuildings or barn; the First Day report instead says the barn and brick house were burned
- `NPSX-NRCA-2017-p129-01` The 1863 woodlots: open-grown white oak, used as pastures; woodlots were important resources before the battle (NPS-NRCA-2017 p. 97): The report says forested woodlots were important resources for the residents before the battle and that open-grown white oak was the dominant vegetation in the 1863 woodlots that were being used as pastures; the same report names a dense understory in woodlots as the 1863 condition to maintain (its context quote), so the density of the 1863 understory is carried as a conflict
- `NPSX-NRCA-2017-p199-01` Management objective: maintain the landscape as it existed in the 1863 battle, with a dense understory in woodlots as the example (NPS-NRCA-2017 p. 167): The report says management objectives of the deer program include maintaining the landscape as it existed during the 1863 battle, giving a dense understory in woodlots as the example (and a patchwork of crop fields at EISE in Eisenhower's time); its forest chapter says instead that the 1863 woodlots were open-grown white oak used as pastures, so this is carried as a conflict
- `NPSX-COMMON-PRIDE-1-p155-01` The board fences along the Emmitsburg Road were still mostly standing when the 56th Virginia reached the road (a soldier's account) (NPS-COMMON-PRIDE-1 p. 139): The study quotes a Virginian's account that when his regiment struck the road the board fences were still mostly standing and caused a momentary check until the men went against and over them; another passage of the study says the road fences near Codori's house were nearly destroyed the day before, so the condition of the road fences during the charge is carried as a conflict

## Rights notes (sources not authored by Service staff, or whose status is not established)

- `NPS-MON-LOC-1993`: Compiled by a park historian with a cooperating association; openly readable. Compiled by Kathy Georg Harrison (Gettysburg National Military Park) with the Eastern National Park and Monument Association; whether the compilation is a United States government work is not established by the document itself; no text of it is quoted
- `NPS-HSR-MCCLEAN-BARN`: Prepared for the National Park Service by consultants and published by it; openly readable. The authors are consulting engineers and architects (Holt, Dickey), not Service employees: whether the work is a United States government work (public domain) is not established by the document itself; short verbatim quotations with citation are used; the owner confirms before any wider reuse
- `NPS-NRCA-2017`: Prepared for the National Park Service by a university author (University of Rhode Island) and published by it as a Natural Resource Report; openly readable. The author is not a Service employee: whether the report is a United States government work is not established by the document itself; short verbatim quotations with citation are used; the owner confirms before any wider reuse
- `NPS-DESIGN-GUIDE`: Not established as a United States government work. Prepared in 1997 for the Gettysburg Historic Architectural Review Board (Borough of Gettysburg) by Margaret M. M. Pickart and Richard C. Sutter & Associates, financed in part with federal funds from the National Park Service (PDF p. 6): a borough design guide hosted on npshistory.com; no text of it is quoted in any extract; a lead only
